1.Gardoš Tower
A red-brick 1896 memorial tower crowning Zemun's old hilltop quarter, built to mark a thousand years of Hungarian settlement on the Pannonian plain and now the best Danube viewpoint in Belgrade.

Local Tastes
Rakija
Serbia's national spirit, a fruit brandy — most often plum, šljivovica — distilled at home or commercially and poured as a welcome drink before nearly any meal.
Rakia Bar
Burek
A flaky, baked filo pastry filled with cheese, meat, or spinach, eaten for breakfast countrywide and judged by Belgraders on crust and filling alone.
Pekara Trpković
Ćevapi
Grilled minced-meat rolls served in flatbread with raw onion and kajmak, the everyday grilled-meat staple of Belgrade's kafanas and fast-food counters alike.
Drama Ćevapi
Food Delivery
Wolt
Foreign number: accepted. — the sign-up form takes any country code and the SMS code arrives over international roaming.
Wolt covers the widest restaurant selection in central Belgrade with reliable live courier tracking; delivery fees run a bit higher than Glovo's on short, in-town hops.
wolt.com
Glovo
Foreign number: accepted. — the sign-up form takes any country code and the SMS code arrives over international roaming.
Glovo, having absorbed the former domestic platform Donesi, covers restaurants, groceries and pharmacy items across Belgrade at competitive fees, with weekend surge pricing the main drawback.
glovoapp.com

Getting Around
CarGo
Foreign number: not accepted. — sign-up requires a Serbian number and foreign numbers are frequently rejected outright; support can register one by email instead.
CarGo is Belgrade's dominant ride-hailing app, with fast pickups and in-app card payment, but the Serbian-number requirement makes it awkward on a short visit — a local SIM or a hotel-booked taxi is often simpler.
appcargo.com
Yandex Go
Foreign number: not accepted. — SMS codes are routed to Russian and CIS numbers only; a foreign number can instead sign in through Yandex's Google login option.
Yandex Go covers Belgrade with metered fares and live driver tracking, and rides can also be booked by phone without the app — but the standard SMS sign-up shuts out most foreign travelers.
go.yandex/en_rs
Tram
All trams, buses and trolleybuses became fare-free citywide, part of a nationwide public-transport policy shift.
Belgrade has a tram system — operated by GSP Beograd. Line used on this trip: 5.
gsp.rs

Day Trips by Train
Novi Sad · 46 min
Serbia's laid-back second city, with an Austro-Hungarian old town around Trg Slobode, the hilltop Petrovaradin Fortress over the Danube, and the EXIT festival every July. Fast direct trains run roughly every 30 minutes, making this the easiest day trip to take.
book at: Srbija Voz or Omio
Sremski Karlovci · 60 min
A small baroque wine town on the Danube just past Novi Sad, its main square ringed by 18th-century landmarks — the Four Lions Fountain, the Patriarch's Palace — with cellars pouring Bermet, a historic dessert wine once served on the Titanic.
book at: Srbija Voz or Omio
Valjevo · 75 min
A quieter inland town on the Kolubara River, built around the cobbled Tešnjar quarter of 19th-century craft workshops, with the ruins of Valjevo Fortress and a National Museum covering the region's role in Serbia's 1804 uprising.
book at: Srbija Voz or Omio
Subotica · 90 min
Serbia's Art Nouveau showcase near the Hungarian border, with a flamboyant City Hall, the pastel Raichle Palace, and a 1902 synagogue built in the same style — plus Lake Palić just outside town for an afternoon by the water.
book at: Srbija Voz or Omio
Vršac · 105 min
The center of Serbia's oldest wine region, planted by Alsatian settlers 300 years ago, with a compact old town beneath the Cathedral of Saint Gerhard and family wineries pouring Rhine Riesling just outside the station.
book at: Srbija Voz or Omio

Worth Knowing

A capital that wears its layers openly

Belgrade has been leveled and rebuilt more than forty times across its history, sitting as it does on the invasion route between the Ottoman and Habsburg empires — Celtic, Roman, Byzantine, Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian and Yugoslav layers all show through in the same few blocks, sometimes on the same building.

A splav is a barge converted into a bar or club, moored along the Sava and Danube riverbanks, and they are Belgrade's signature night out rather than a tourist gimmick — locals pick a splav by its music policy — folk, house, turbo-folk — as carefully as they'd pick a restaurant.

Serbian is written officially in both Cyrillic and Latin script, and the two alternate on street signs, menus and storefronts with no fixed pattern — it is not a bug or an inconsistency, just how the language is actually used day to day.

Cards are widely accepted in restaurants and shops, but many kafanas, market stalls and smaller cafés still run cash-only or prefer it, and dinar notes are easiest to come by from a bank ATM rather than a currency exchange counter.
